'''Foodo''' ([[ISO 639-3]] fod) is a [[Guang language]] spoken in and around the town of [[Sèmèrè]] in the north of [[Benin]]. There are approximately 37,000 speakers (taking the most recent estimate and adding the estimated 3.2% a year growth rate for [[Benin]]<ref>Alexandratos, N. (ed.) (1995). World Agriculture Towards 2010: An FAO Study. New York: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and John Wiley and Sons.</ref>). A large proportion of the population live beyond the homeland in other parts of [[Benin]], as well as in neighboring [[Togo]], [[Nigeria]], and [[Ghana]]. There may be as many as 1,000 living in [[Ghana]].

The language has its origin in [[Ghana]]. Approximately 200 to 300 years ago, a group of [[Guang languages|Guang]] speakers migrated from the south of [[Ghana]] to [[Sèmèrè]] along the ancient cola trade route which extended through [[Togo]] and [[Benin]] to [[Nigeria]].<ref>Cornevin, Robert. 1964. Contribution à l'etude des populations parlant des langues gouang au Togo et au Dahomey. Journal of African Languages 3:226-230.</ref><ref>Bertho, J. 1951. Trois îlots linguistiques du Moyen-Dahomey: le Tshummbuli, le Bazantché, et le Basila. Bulletin de l'Institut Français d'Afrique Noire, 13:872-892.</ref> The various origins of Foodo speakers are still retained in clan names."<ref>Plunkett, Gray C. 2009. An overview of Foodo, a linguistic island in Benin. Journal of West African Languages, 36:1-2.107-137.</ref>

==Sociolinguistic background==
Foodo is one of the [[national language]]s of [[Benin]]. In the [[Beninese]] sociopolitical context 'national language' is interpreted to mean all [[Languages of Africa|African language]]s spoken within the borders of the country.

The Foodo have close historical and cultural links through [[Islam]] to the [[Tem (Togo tribe)|Tem]] (often known as [[Kotokoli]]), in and around the town of [[Sokode]] in [[Togo]]. Many Foodo are bilingual in [[Tem language|Tem]] as a [[trade language]].

===Tones===
Foodo is a [[tonal language]], meaning that [[pitch accent|pitch]] differences are used to distinguish one word from another. These contrasts may be [[exical form|lexical]] or [[grammatical]].

There are two [[tone (linguistics)|tone]]s, High (H) and Low (L).

Foodo also has automatic [[downstep]], where a H following a L is always pronounced on a lower [[pitch (music)|pitch]] than the preceding H within the same [[phonological phrase]]. Numerous [[tonal processes]] occur once words are placed in context.<ref>Plunkett, Gray C. (1991). The tone system of Foodo nouns: University of North Dakota. Masters thesis.</ref>

===Syllable structure===
In underlying forms, there are five possible [[syllable]] types: CV, CV:, CVV, CVC, V and VC. Except for some [[pronominal]] forms, both V and VC are limited to [[affix]]es. The only [[consonant]]s which occur in the coda position are [[nasal stop|nasals]].<ref>Plunkett, Gray C. 2009. An overview of Foodo, a linguistic island in Benin. Journal of West African Languages, 36:1-2.114.</ref>

===Vowel harmony===
Foodo has [[vowel harmony]]. All [[vowels]] in the [[Word stem|stem]] agree in regard to their [[Advanced tongue root|ATR]] quality. [[Prefix]]es and most [[suffix]]es receive their [[Advanced tongue root|ATR]] feature from the [[Advanced tongue root|ATR]] quality of the [[Word stem|stem]]. There is also some [[rounding]] [[vowel harmony]] in [[nouns]], but this is more restrictive and often varies between speakers.<ref>Plunkett, Gray C. 2009. An overview of Foodo, a linguistic island in Benin. Journal of West African Languages, 36:1-2.112.</ref>

==Orthography==
The Foodo [[orthography]] uses modified [[Roman script]], adding various characters to represent sounds that do not occur in [[European languages]].<ref name="autogenerated1998">Zakari, Aboubakari & Gray Plunkett (1998). Guide pour lire et écrire le foodo, édition préliminaire. Sèmèrè par Djougou, Bénin: Commission Nationale de Linguistique Foodo en collaboration avec SIL.</ref>

===Tones===
The Foodo [[orthography]] marks an [[acute accent]] on the first [[syllable]] of the [[word]] if that [[syllable]] is H tone, and leaves all other [[syllable]]s unmarked. e.g.á é ɛ́ í ɩ́ ó ɔ́ ú ʊ́<ref name="autogenerated1998"/>

==Grammar==

===Noun classes===
Foodo has ten [[noun class]]es. Most [[noun]]s consist of a [[Word stem|stem]] with a [[noun class]] [[prefix]] and a [[noun class]] [[suffix]]. But it is more helpful to speak of classification being based on [[agreement (linguistics)|agreement]] patterns rather than just on the form of a single [[affix]]. [[Noun]]s are grouped into different sets which share common [[agreement (linguistics)|agreement]] phenomena within the [[noun phrase]] and on concordant [[anaphoric pronoun]]s outside the [[noun phrase]]. The [[tone (linguistics)|tone]] on [[noun class]] [[prefix]]es behaves similarly to other [[Guang languages]].<ref>Snider, Keith 1990b. Tone in proto-Guang nouns. African Languages and Cultures 3.1:87-105</ref>

===Syntax===
Foodo is an [[Subject–verb–object|SVO]] language. [[Adverbial phrases]] are generally [[clause]] final. The order of [[morphemes]] within a verbal word is: [[subject (grammar)|subject]] [[anaphora (linguistics)|anaphoric]] [[clitic]] — [[Affirmative and negative|negative]] marker — [[Tense–aspect–mood|TAM]] — [[verb]] [[Word stem|stem]] — directional].<ref>Plunkett, Gray C. 2009. An overview of Foodo, a linguistic island in Benin. Journal of West African Languages, 36:1-2.114-115.</ref>
